blocks.p: Rei started with the sixth name, because Higuchi had starred it twice in the margin. Watanabe Jun, Despair VI, weakening. The other names were still only words on a page. A weakening holder was different. He was a real man somewhere in the city, and Rei could help him or hurt him just by knocking on the wrong door.

He had not slept. In the late afternoon he left the flat and walked to Jūjō station through heat that pressed on the back of his neck like a hand. The cicadas were screaming in every tree along the way. On the green-striped Saikyō line train to Ikebukuro, a schoolgirl in a summer uniform slept against her friend's shoulder, and the friend held very still so as not to wake her. At Ikebukuro he changed to the Tōbu Tōjō line and rode out west, past rooftops hung with drying futons, to a small station called Tokiwadai.

The pencilled note had sent him to this quiet corner of Itabashi. The streets here had been planned in the 1930s. They were straight and tidy and lined with old trees, and they curved around in neat loops. Very little happened here on the other side of the veil. Gin's book had a word for ground like this. It called it clean. The Grid kept safe houses here for practitioners who needed to think without noise. Rei understood at once why a man carrying Despair would choose to live in the quietest ground he could find.

Watanabe Jun was not what Rei had expected. Rei had been carrying the word holder around all day like a heavy stone. He had pictured someone large. Instead he found a slight man in a cardigan two sizes too big, shelving returned books at the local public library. He looked fifty. The file said thirty-five. He had the quiet gentleness of a person who has decided not to take up much room in the world.

Rei took a newspaper from the rack, sat down in the periodicals corner and watched him for an hour. The air conditioning hummed. A student was asleep over his textbooks. A woman in a sun hat returned a stack of romance novels and left. Nothing about Watanabe was strange except the light around him. It was a little dimmer near him, a half-step darker, the way a room goes dim when a cloud passes the window. But there was no cloud. And Rei noticed that nobody ever quite met his eyes. Not the student. Not the woman with the novels.
Rei watched him put a novel back on its shelf with both hands, as if it were much heavier than it was. Then he understood. He was looking at the price of the seat, written plainly on a living man.

A holder did not use his domain like a power. He stood inside it, the way a person stands out in bad weather, so that nobody else had to stand in it. Watanabe had been given Despair. Rei did not know how. Perhaps by chance, perhaps it was handed down, perhaps he had offered himself. Whatever the reason, the weight had worn him thin, the way running water wears down a stone. It did not happen all at once. It happened every day. Now the man was mostly the shape of the thing he carried, with only a little person left over to do the carrying.

Higuchi's word was weakening, and now Rei could see it. Watanabe's hands trembled on the books. In the poor library light, the edges of him looked almost see-through. And Rei understood why. It was not his age. It was the empty thirteenth seat in Kita, two wards away. That empty chair was pulling on the full ones around it. Watanabe's seat was the nearest to the wound, so it was pulled the hardest. For six years the empty chair had been leaning on him and borrowing his strength.

At last Watanabe noticed Rei watching. People who live with something strange always notice in the end. Rei expected him to look afraid. Instead Watanabe gave him a small, tired nod. He did not know Rei's face. But he knew Rei's kind. The kind who could see the dimmed light.
He came over and spoke very quietly, so that the sleeping student would not wake.

"I've been wondering when one of you would come," he said. "If you have a moment, and you are what I think you are, I'd like to know something. On the worst nights I've started to feel a thirteenth weight leaning on my sixth. And I've started to feel that something kind and patient, over in Kita, has begun very gently to help it lean. Is that true?"

Rei had not come to tell a dying man the name of the thing that was killing him. But this man was holding Despair for the whole north of the city, and he had asked an honest question. His cardigan was two sizes too big because there was less of him inside it every week.
"Yes," Rei said. "It's true. The thing helping it lean is wearing my brother."
Watanabe closed his eyes for a moment. When he opened them, there was no surprise in them. There was only a kind of tired thanks.
"Then I'm sorry for you," he said. "That's worse than what's happening to me."

Rei could not visit all twelve. There was no time. Some of the names lived in places he had no way to reach. One of them was the eleventh, Park Junho, who held Longing. He was listed at the community centre in Shin-Ōkubo, with a note in Gin's hand that Rei did not understand yet. Pak Sun-ja keeps his secret. The note did not say what the secret was.

But he saw four more before the first trains started running again. He rode the Saikyō line back to Jūjō as the sky went dark, among tired office workers with their ties loosened and their phones glowing in their hands. Then he walked. Now that he knew what a leaning chair looked like, he could not stop seeing them. The whole city seemed to arrange itself around what he could see.

In Kita, down an alley behind a public bath, a boiler-room door was propped open to let the heat out. Inside, a big man in dark clothes was feeding a firebox one shovel of fuel at a time. His hair was cropped short, dark with some grey in it. Every movement he made was held down to the smallest size it could be. No wasted gesture. No slammed door. Rei did not go in. He was not even sure this was the right man, because Gin's file said the second holder was hard to find on purpose. But he watched him work for a long minute. The man looked like a whole life built into one careful shape, a shape that gave his weather somewhere to go where it would hurt no one. The heat poured off the firebox and never seemed to reach his hands. He looked like a holder who had made his peace. Even so, while Rei watched, he glanced north twice, the way a man checks a sky he does not trust.

blocks.cap: Hoshino Haru, holder of Joy, at his stockpot

blocks.p: On Sakae Street, at two in the morning, the light was still on in a small noodle shop. Through the steamed-up glass Rei could see a stocky man in an apron skimming the top of a big stockpot. The broth took eight hours, Gin had written. This was Hoshino Haru, who held Joy, the seventh seat. His teacher had passed it to him so smoothly that it was the cleanest handover on record. Rei stood across the street for a while and simply felt it. It was the warmest thing he had felt all month, the plain happiness of something good done well. And yet, even here, the steam from the pot drifted north, though there was no wind to carry it.

Outside a pale danchi he looked up. A danchi is a big public housing block, built by the thousand after the war, rows and rows of the same small flats with the same steel doors. On the half-landing of an outside stairwell sat a woman at three in the morning. Her knees were pulled up to her chest. She was not climbing. Fear, the fourth seat. She had not climbed her own stairs in days.

After that Rei walked south beside the Keihin-Tōhoku tracks, toward the centre of the city. The last trains had gone. The rails were silent and the signals glowed red over empty platforms. Vending machines hummed on every corner, lighting the pavement white. A taxi went by slowly with its little red light on, looking for anyone still out. By Ueno station the late counters were still open. A lean man paid for a plate he had not finished, and he was gone before the cook had counted his change. Hunger, the ninth seat. He never stayed anywhere long enough to finish a plate.
Each of them was ordinary in the same way. Each of them was a person who had built a whole life around a weight that could never be put down.
And over that long night, Rei came to understand that each of them was leaning the same way.
Not toward each other. Toward the gap.

Higuchi's note had explained how it was meant to work. Twelve holders, spread around the table, should balance each other. That way no single part of the veil had to carry more than it could bear. For a century, the note said, it had balanced. But a table with one chair pulled out begins to tilt. Every plate on it slides, slowly, toward the empty place.

The man at the boiler checked the northern sky because Rage felt the empty chair as a heat that would not quite die down. The woman on the stairs felt it as a fear with nothing to be afraid of. Watanabe felt it most, because his seat was the nearest and the weakest. But all twelve of them felt it. It was a low, constant pull toward Kita, where a chair had stood empty since the year the city went grey. None of them had the power to fill it. None of them was free to leave their own seat. And none of them, Rei realised, had ever been told why the weather they had carried all their lives had lately been getting worse.

When the first trains began to run, Rei took one north from Ueno. The car was nearly empty. A young man in a crumpled host's suit slept with his mouth open. An old woman held a cloth bundle of flowers and fruit on her knees, an offering for a family grave. Rei rode north with his forehead against the cool glass and watched the sky go from black to grey.

He had not eaten. Near the station a bakery opened at five. Rei stood outside the Akebono Bakery while a woman in her late fifties raised the metal shutter and set out the first trays of bread. The window glowed yellow, and the smell of warm butter came out onto the empty street.

A man was already waiting. He was neat and ordinary, with gold wire glasses and his collar one button open. The baker handed him a paper bag without being asked. He thanked her, and for the few seconds she spoke to him, she looked like the only person in the world. Then Rei saw that it went the other way too. The man was looking at her as if she were the only person in the world. He was not putting it on. It was simply what his attention did.
Sakuma Kei, Rei thought. Love. The third seat. The most stable of all the thirteen domains. The dawn regular whom Mrs. Kawai fed.

Kei walked past Rei on the pavement. For a moment he glanced at him through the gold frames with a strange, kind attention, as if he had just recognised some bond Rei carried. Then he nodded politely and went on toward the station. He did not look north at all. Rei would remember that. The steadiest of them did not look north. He just walked a little faster.

Rei stopped on the small bridge over the river near home as the light came up. Gin's book was in his bag, with the list of holders copied into the back. Twelve names. Twelve kinds of weather. And one wound.
What frightened him was not how strong the far shore was. It was how reasonable the Healer's plan looked from here.

Twelve people were being slowly crushed by an empty chair. As far as Rei could understand it that night, one demon, patient and kind, was offering to end the leaning. To fill the gap. To let Watanabe put down the weight that was killing him. To let the man at the boiler finally let his fire die down.

And the price? The thing in that chair would not be a person carrying a feeling inside for the city's sake. It would be a feeling wearing a person on the outside, for its own sake. The body it meant to do this in was Gin's. And the hand it had spent a month shaping to fit the seat was Rei's.

The trap had never been that the plan was evil. The trap was that, seen from a bridge at dawn with a dying librarian behind him, the plan looked like mercy. Rei was the only one in a position to refuse it. And if he refused, twelve people would go on leaning into a gap he had just told one of them was real.
